evidence: Cic. Mur. 76: ōdit populus Rōmānus prīvātam luxuriam (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Lavish living and spending, usually with disapproval: Cicero sets private luxuria against public magnificentia. Its first sense is the rank growth of plants (Verg. G. 1.112).

evidence: Ter. Ad. 4.7.42: adulēscēns luxū perditus (Lewis & Short)
Verg. A. 1.637: rēgālī splendida luxū (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Like luxuria, of excess in eating and drinking; in Virgil also, without blame, royal splendour.

evidence: Cic. Fam. 9.16.8: fāma ad tē dē meā novā lautitiā veniet (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The elegance of a well-kept house and a good table, without the moral blame of luxuria; Cicero uses it of himself, joking.

evidence: Cic. Mur. 13: multārum dēliciārum comes est extrēma saltātiō (Lewis & Short)
M-O s.v. enjoy: live it up (in dēliciīs vīvere)
terms.comment: Things that delight the senses; in dēliciīs vīvere is “to live in luxury” (Vulg. Apoc. 18.9, cited by Morgan–Owens). The same word is also “darling” (dēliciae meae).
Of people and their way of life, extravagant; of crops, rank. For a luxurious thing, lautus (elegant, sumptuous) or sūmptuōsus (costly) is often the better word.

phrases.latin: licet enim sine luxuriā agere fēstum diem
phrases.english: for you can keep a holiday without extravagance

phrases.latin: multa et lauta supellex, nōn illa quidem luxuriōsī hominis, sed tamen abundantis
phrases.english: plenty of fine furniture, not that of a man of luxury, but of one who had more than enough
